claim: We hypothesize that free_sulfur_dioxide is positively monotonic associated with total_sulfur_dioxide (Spearman rho = 0.798, p < 1e-246). This indicates that wines with higher free sulfur dioxide concentrations also tend to have higher total sulfur dioxide, reflecting a consistent sulfur profile across samples.

We hypothesize that fixed_acidity is negatively linearly associated with pH (Pearson r = -0.678, p < 1e-150). Higher fixed acidity corresponds to lower pH values, reflecting the expected acid-base balance in red wine.

We hypothesize that fixed_acidity is positively linearly associated with citric_acid (Pearson r = 0.661, p < 1e-140). This suggests that wines with higher fixed acidity also tend to contain more citric acid, indicating a coordinated acid composition.

We hypothesize that fixed_acidity is positively linearly associated with density (Pearson r = 0.657, p < 1e-138). Higher fixed acidity appears to increase wine density, reflecting the contribution of dissolved acids to mass per volume.

We hypothesize that volatile_acidity is negatively linearly associated with citric_acid (Pearson r = -0.551, p < 1e-89). Wines with higher volatile acidity tend to have lower citric acid levels, indicating a trade‑off between these two acid components.
We hypothesize that citric_acid is negatively linearly associated with pH (Pearson r = -0.533, p < 1e-82). Higher citric acid concentrations lower the pH, consistent with its acidic nature.

We hypothesize that alcohol content is positively linearly associated with wine quality (Pearson r = 0.492, p < 1e-68). Higher alcohol levels tend to correspond to higher quality ratings in the dataset.

We hypothesize that density is negatively linearly associated with alcohol (Pearson r = -0.473, p < 1e-62). As alcohol concentration rises, wine density tends to decrease, reflecting alcohol's lower density relative to water.

We hypothesize that residual_sugar is positively monotonic associated with density (Spearman rho = 0.429, p < 1e-50). Higher residual sugar levels correspond to higher wine density, likely due to the added mass of sugars.
We hypothesize that sulphates are positively monotonic associated with quality (Spearman rho = 0.389, p < 1e-41). Wines with higher sulphate concentrations tend to receive higher quality scores.

We hypothesize that volatile_acidity is negatively linearly associated with quality (Pearson r = -0.384, p < 1e-40). Higher volatile acidity corresponds to lower quality ratings, reflecting its detrimental sensory impact.

We hypothesize that volatile_acidity is negatively monotonic associated with sulphates (Spearman rho = -0.349, p < 1e-32). Higher volatile acidity tends to co‑occur with lower sulphate levels, suggesting an inverse relationship between these components.

We hypothesize that fixed_acidity is simultaneously positively associated with density and citric_acid, and negatively associated with pH, reflecting a coordinated acid‑density‑pH pattern (supported by edges E2, E3, E4). This pattern suggests that higher fixed acidity drives both higher density and citric acid content while lowering pH, indicating a linked chemical profile.

We hypothesize that wine quality is jointly positively associated with alcohol and sulphates, and negatively associated with volatile_acidity (edges E7, E10, E11), indicating that higher alcohol and sulphate levels improve perceived quality while higher volatile acidity detracts from it.

We hypothesize that density is positively associated with residual_sugar, total_sulfur_dioxide, and free_sulfur_dioxide (edges E1, E9), suggesting that higher sugar and sulfur compound concentrations increase wine density.

We hypothesize that citric_acid is positively associated with fixed_acidity and negatively associated with both volatile_acidity and pH (edges E3, E5, E6), reflecting a pattern where higher citric acid coincides with higher fixed acidity but lower volatile acidity and pH.

We hypothesize that volatile_acidity is negatively associated with sulphates and quality, and positively associated with citric_acid (edges E5, E11, E12), indicating that higher volatile acidity coincides with lower sulphate levels and lower quality, while aligning with higher citric acid.
